courses.title: Paediatrics II: Childhood Illness and IMCI
courses.description: Integrated management of childhood illness, pneumonia, diarrhoea, severe malaria, meningitis, sickle cell disease, HIV, heart and kidney disease in children, and emergency triage.

topics.title: IMCI and Emergency Triage
topics.summary: ETAT emergency signs, IMCI danger signs and classification, and paediatric emergencies.

material.heading: Triage
material.body: Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment (ETAT) sorts sick children into emergency (E), priority (P) and queue. Emergency signs (ABCD): obstructed or absent breathing, severe respiratory distress, central cyanosis, signs of shock (cold hands with capillary refill > 3 seconds and weak fast pulse), coma, convulsions, and severe dehydration (lethargy, sunken eyes, very slow skin pinch) in a child with diarrhoea. Priority signs (3 TPR MOB): tiny baby, temperature (very high), trauma, pallor (severe), poisoning, pain (severe), respiratory distress, restless/irritable/lethargic, referral (urgent), malnutrition (visible severe wasting), oedema of both feet, burns. Treatments: airway positioning, oxygen, IV/IO fluids for shock (10–20 mL/kg crystalloid, caution in severe malnutrition and severe anaemia), 10% dextrose 5 mL/kg for hypoglycaemia, and anticonvulsants (rectal or IV diazepam, or buccal midazolam).
keyPoints: Shock: cold hands, CRT > 3 s, weak fast pulse

material.heading: IMCI
material.body: Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI — for children 2 months to 5 years) uses a standard approach: check general danger signs (unable to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargic or unconscious) — any sign means urgent referral; then assess main symptoms (cough or difficult breathing, diarrhoea, fever, ear problem), nutrition and anaemia, immunisation, vitamin A and deworming status, and other problems. Classifications use colour codes: pink (urgent referral after pre-referral treatment), yellow (specific treatment at the clinic), green (home care). Counselling mothers on feeding, fluids and when to return is integral. Community-based IMCI (iCCM) enables trained community health workers to treat malaria (RDT + ACT), pneumonia (amoxicillin) and diarrhoea (ORS + zinc) in hard-to-reach areas.

topics.title: Pneumonia and Diarrhoeal Disease
topics.summary: Assessment and treatment of childhood pneumonia, bronchiolitis, and diarrhoea and dehydration.

material.heading: Pneumonia
material.body: Pneumonia is a leading killer of Nigerian under-fives (Nigeria has the highest number of child pneumonia deaths globally). IMCI classification: fast breathing (≥ 50/min at 2–11 months; ≥ 40/min at 12–59 months) and/or chest indrawing — pneumonia treated with oral amoxicillin (dispersible, 5 days, or 3 days in low-HIV settings); any general danger sign or severe respiratory distress, SpO2 < 90% or central cyanosis — severe pneumonia requiring admission, oxygen and injectable antibiotics (ampicillin/penicillin plus gentamicin; ceftriaxone second-line). Pulse oximetry and reliable oxygen supply (concentrators, solar-powered systems) save lives. Causes: pneumococcus and Hib (vaccines reduce these), Staphylococcus aureus (post-measles; pneumatoceles, empyema), RSV and other viruses; consider TB and PCP in HIV-exposed infants. Bronchiolitis (RSV, infants < 1 year): wheeze and crackles, supportive care (oxygen, feeding, nasal suction) — antibiotics and bronchodilators are not routinely needed. Risk factors: malnutrition, lack of breastfeeding, indoor smoke, crowding, HIV.

material.heading: Diarrhoea and dehydration
material.body: Diarrhoea is another leading cause of child death. Assess dehydration: no dehydration (Plan A — extra fluids, ORS, continue feeding, zinc 10–14 days: 10 mg < 6 months, 20 mg ≥ 6 months), some dehydration (restless/irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, skin pinch goes back slowly — Plan B: 75 mL/kg ORS over 4 hours), severe dehydration (lethargic/unconscious, sunken eyes, drinks poorly, skin pinch goes back very slowly — Plan C: IV Ringer's lactate 100 mL/kg — in infants 30 mL/kg over 1 hour then 70 mL/kg over 5 hours; children ≥ 12 months 30 mL/kg over 30 minutes then 70 mL/kg over 2½ hours). Dysentery (blood in stool — Shigella): ciprofloxacin. Persistent diarrhoea (≥ 14 days) needs nutritional management and HIV testing. Antidiarrhoeal and antiemetic drugs are not recommended. Prevention: rotavirus vaccine, exclusive breastfeeding, safe water, handwashing, sanitation and vitamin A.
keyPoints: Plan B: 75 mL/kg ORS over 4 h

topics.title: Severe Malaria, Meningitis and Measles
topics.summary: Paediatric severe malaria, bacterial meningitis, measles and its complications.

material.heading: Severe malaria and meningitis
material.body: Severe malaria in children commonly presents as cerebral malaria (coma, convulsions), severe anaemia (Hb < 5 g/dL — transfuse 20 mL/kg whole blood or 10 mL/kg packed cells), respiratory distress (metabolic acidosis — deep breathing), hypoglycaemia and prostration. Treat with IV/IM artesunate (3 mg/kg for children < 20 kg), correct hypoglycaemia, treat convulsions, cautious fluids (avoid boluses unless shocked — FEAST trial), transfuse when indicated, and give antibiotics if bacterial co-infection is suspected (non-typhoidal Salmonella bacteraemia is common). Pre-referral rectal artesunate in the community. Neurological sequelae can follow cerebral malaria. Bacterial meningitis in children (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib; in neonates GBS, E. coli): fever, bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness (unreliable in infants), convulsions, altered consciousness; lumbar puncture unless contraindicated; ceftriaxone; complications include hearing loss (test all survivors), hydrocephalus, subdural effusions and seizures.

material.heading: Measles
material.body: Measles remains a major childhood killer in Nigeria due to low vaccine coverage (large outbreaks, especially in the north). Features: prodrome of high fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis ('3 Cs'), Koplik spots (white spots on the buccal mucosa), then a maculopapular rash starting behind the ears and spreading down the body, fading with desquamation. Complications: pneumonia (the commonest cause of death), diarrhoea, malnutrition (measles precipitates kwashiorkor), otitis media, croup, keratitis and corneal ulceration (blindness — especially with vitamin A deficiency), encephalitis, and later subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). Measles causes immune amnesia, increasing risk of other infections for months. Management: vitamin A (on days 1 and 2 — 50,000 IU < 6 months, 100,000 IU 6–11 months, 200,000 IU ≥ 12 months; a third dose if eye signs), treat complications, nutrition, and isolate. Prevention: two doses of measles-containing vaccine (9 and 15 months) and outbreak response.

topics.title: Sickle Cell Disease and HIV in Children
topics.summary: Paediatric sickle cell complications and prevention, and paediatric HIV care.

material.heading: Sickle cell disease
material.body: About 150,000 Nigerian babies are born with sickle cell disease yearly; without care, many die before age 5 (infection, splenic sequestration, anaemia). Early presentations: dactylitis (hand–foot syndrome — painful swollen hands and feet in infants 6 months–2 years), bacterial infections (pneumococcus — functional asplenia; Salmonella osteomyelitis), acute splenic sequestration (sudden enlarging spleen with falling Hb and shock — transfusion; teach parents to palpate the spleen), acute chest syndrome, stroke (screen with transcranial Doppler — TCD velocity ≥ 200 cm/s indicates high risk; hydroxyurea or transfusion), and aplastic crises. Comprehensive care: newborn screening and early diagnosis, penicillin V prophylaxis until at least 5 years, pneumococcal and other vaccines, folic acid, malaria chemoprophylaxis, hydroxyurea from 9 months (reduces crises, ACS and mortality — increasingly recommended in Africa), hydration and prompt analgesia, parent education, and genetic counselling.

material.heading: Paediatric HIV
material.body: Most paediatric HIV results from mother-to-child transmission (in pregnancy, during delivery or through breastfeeding); Nigeria has one of the largest numbers of children living with HIV. PMTCT: maternal ART, infant prophylaxis (nevirapine ± zidovudine for 6–12 weeks), safe breastfeeding on ART, and early infant diagnosis (DNA PCR at 6 weeks, then after breastfeeding cessation; antibody tests at 18 months). All children diagnosed with HIV start ART promptly (dolutegravir-based regimens; paediatric DTG 10 mg dispersible tablets) with cotrimoxazole prophylaxis. Clinical features: failure to thrive, recurrent infections, oral thrush, persistent diarrhoea, lymphadenopathy, parotid enlargement, developmental delay and TB. Adolescents living with HIV need support for adherence, disclosure, transition to adult care and sexual and reproductive health.

topics.title: Heart, Kidney and Neurological Disorders in Children
topics.summary: Congenital heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, nephrotic and nephritic syndromes, febrile seizures and epilepsy.

material.heading: Heart and kidney
material.body: Congenital heart disease (about 8 per 1,000 births): acyanotic (VSD — the commonest, holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge; ASD; PDA — continuous machinery murmur, more common in preterms) and cyanotic (tetralogy of Fallot — VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, RVH; hypercyanotic 'tet' spells treated with knee–chest position, oxygen, morphine; transposition of the great arteries — cyanosis at birth). Signs of heart failure in infants: fast breathing, sweating and breathlessness during feeds, poor weight gain, hepatomegaly. Surgery is available in few Nigerian centres, and many children travel abroad or die untreated. Rheumatic heart disease in school-age children follows rheumatic fever. Nephrotic syndrome (oedema, heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia): minimal change disease commonest globally (steroid-responsive), though steroid-resistant forms and secondary causes (quartan malaria, hepatitis B, HIV) are relatively more common in Nigeria; treat with prednisolone. Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: haematuria (cola-coloured urine), oedema, hypertension 1–3 weeks after throat or skin infection; low C3; supportive care.

material.heading: Neurology
material.body: Febrile seizures occur between 6 months and 5 years with fever (not due to CNS infection): simple (generalised, < 15 minutes, once in 24 hours) have an excellent prognosis; complex (focal, prolonged, recurrent) need further evaluation. Always exclude meningitis and cerebral malaria (lumbar puncture in infants and when signs are present). Management: treat fever cause, parent education; antipyretics do not prevent recurrence. Epilepsy in children: absence seizures (brief staring, 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG — ethosuximide or valproate), infantile spasms (West syndrome — hypsarrhythmia), and focal epilepsies; stigma and school exclusion are problems in Nigeria. Other conditions: cerebral palsy (non-progressive; multidisciplinary rehabilitation), hydrocephalus, neural tube defects, and post-infectious sequelae (after meningitis, cerebral malaria, kernicterus). Acute flaccid paralysis in a child must be reported for polio surveillance.
